13% of trading days drive more than 60% of the annual equity premium. The calendar is published 12 months in advance.

This is the Macro Announcement Premium. Savor and Wilson, JFQA (2013) and JFE (2014).

Here's the complete logic, no black box:

🔹 ANNOUNCEMENT CALENDAR. FOMC, CPI/PPI, BLS employment. Fully ex-ante known. Pull it from any free macro feed.
🔹 ON/OFF GATE. Hold equity exposure on announcement days. Step out on the rest.
🔹 ANNOUNCEMENT DAY RETURN. Sample averaged 11.4 basis points on the roughly 30 to 40 announcement days each year, versus 1.1 basis points on every other day. From 1958 to 2009.
🔹 SML SLOPES UP. The security market line is upward on announcement days. Beta gets paid. On every other day, it's flat. Risk doesn't get rewarded when nothing is being decided.
🔹 RISK-PREMIUM SOURCE. Compensation for resolving non-diversifiable growth and inflation uncertainty. It's a premium, not a mispricing.
🔹 DAILY REBALANCE. Simple on/off switch. No forecasting. No signal lag.

Source: Savor and Wilson (2013), JFQA 48(2) and (2014), JFE 113(2). Theoretical backing in Ai and Bansal (2018), Econometrica. Educational use only.

Savor and Wilson published a finding in 2013 and 2014 that most retail traders have never heard of.

Roughly 13% of trading days drive more than 60% of the annual US equity premium. And those days are fully ex-ante known, printed on the FOMC, CPI, and BLS employment calendars 12 months in advance.

The complete logic:

🔹 Pull the FOMC, CPI/PPI, and BLS employment release calendar. Roughly 30 to 40 days per year.
🔹 Hold equity exposure on announcement days. Step out on every other day.
🔹 In the 1958 to 2009 sample, announcement days averaged 11.4 basis points versus 1.1 basis points on non-announcement days.
🔹 On announcement days, the security market line slopes upward. Beta gets paid. On every other day, it's flat.
🔹 The premium compensates investors for resolving non-diversifiable growth and inflation uncertainty.
🔹 Daily rebalance. Simple on/off switch. No forecasting required.

Source: Savor and Wilson (2013), JFQA 48(2) and (2014), JFE 113(2). Theoretical backing in Ai and Bansal (2018), Econometrica. Educational use only.
